menstrual.name: Menstrual
menstrual.focus: Replenish iron and minerals lost during bleeding. Choose warm, mineral-rich foods like sea vegetables, mushrooms, dark beans and seafood.
menstrual.framework: Framework direction: warming, mineral-rich foods; sea vegetables, dark beans, seafood; slow-cooked meals. Seeds: sesame and sunflower (seed-cycling convention).

copyReview.note: Menstrual blood loss is a leading cause of low iron in people who menstruate, and their recommended intake is higher (18 vs 8 mg/day). Iron status builds over weeks, so eating iron-rich food all month matters as much as during the period.
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Iron fact sheet: higher iron needs (18 vs 8 mg/day) for people who menstruate; heavy menstrual bleeding as a cause of iron deficiency; vitamin C and tea/coffee effects on non-haem iron

copyReview.note: Iron is the main mineral lost in meaningful amounts. Other minerals aren't significantly depleted by normal bleeding.
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Iron fact sheet: higher iron needs (18 vs 8 mg/day) for people who menstruate; heavy menstrual bleeding as a cause of iron deficiency; vitamin C and tea/coffee effects on non-haem iron

copyReview.note: A warmth or comfort idea (traditional-medicine style), not a nutritional claim. Fine as tone.
Mushrooms aren't a notable iron source. Sea vegetables are mineral-rich but come with iodine (kelp, kombu) and arsenic (hijiki) cautions. Dark beans and shellfish are good examples.
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Iodine fact sheet; EFSA tolerable upper intake for iodine (600 µg/day adults): very high and variable iodine in kelp and kombu
UK Food Standards Agency advice to avoid hijiki seaweed because of its inorganic arsenic content (also advised by food-safety agencies in Canada, Australia/NZ and Hong Kong)

follicular.name: Follicular
follicular.focus: Estrogen is rising and energy returns. Go for fresh, vibrant foods, sprouted grains, lean proteins and fermented foods to support your gut.
follicular.cooking: Light steaming, quick sautés and fresh salads.
follicular.framework: Framework direction: lighter, fresher foods; sprouted grains; fermented and pickled foods; lean protein; light cooking. Seeds: flax and pumpkin (seed-cycling convention).

copyReview.note: Estradiol rises through the follicular phase toward ovulation.
Studies of energy and mood across the cycle are mixed. Gentle editorial wording, not a fact for everyone.
Food suggestion. Don't claim that sprouting boosts nutrients; the evidence is modest and variable.

Fermented-food diets can increase microbiome diversity, but the evidence is still developing. “Can help support” is acceptable; avoid stronger wording. Note that most pickles and all vinegar contain no live cultures.
sources: Wastyk et al., Cell 2021 (fermented-food diet increased gut microbiome diversity); ISAPP consensus statement on fermented foods, Nat Rev Gastroenterol Hepatol 2021: emerging evidence

ovulatory.name: Ovulatory
ovulatory.focus: Energy peaks. Support your liver with fibre-rich vegetables, colourful fruit and anti-inflammatory foods to process the estrogen surge.
ovulatory.cooking: Raw, lightly grilled or quick-cooked meals.
ovulatory.framework: Framework direction: raw and lightly cooked, fibre-rich and colourful foods; cruciferous and bitter greens; presented as supporting the liver and estrogen clearance. Seeds: flax and pumpkin.

copyReview.note: Not consistently shown. Editorial at best.

copyReview.phrase: “Support your liver … to process the estrogen surge”
copyReview.note: There's no good evidence that particular foods help the liver process the mid-cycle estrogen rise, and a healthy liver does this without dietary help. This is the kind of hormone claim the guardrails exclude.
sources: Human studies on cruciferous vegetables / indole-3-carbinol and estrogen metabolites are small and inconsistent, with no clinical outcome evidence for menstrual-cycle effects

copyReview.note: No phase-specific evidence. As general nutrition, colourful plant-rich eating is fine, but avoid presenting foods as treatments.
sources: NCCIH turmeric fact sheet: health-effect evidence is mainly from curcumin supplements, and it's limited; supplements are linked to rare liver injury

copyReview.note: Good general nutrition advice, not specific to ovulation.
Traditional-medicine style tone, no claim.
Recommending alcohol conflicts with WHO advice. Around ovulation, people trying to conceive are advised to avoid it.
sources: WHO (2023): no level of alcohol consumption is safe for health; NHS/ACOG advise avoiding alcohol when trying to conceive or pregnant

luteal.name: Luteal
luteal.focus: Progesterone rises and cravings may appear. Stabilise blood sugar with complex carbs, root vegetables and B-vitamin and magnesium-rich foods.
luteal.cooking: Roasting and baking for comforting, grounding meals.
luteal.framework: Framework direction: complex carbohydrates, roasted root vegetables, B-vitamin and magnesium-rich foods, to address cravings. Seeds: sesame and sunflower.

copyReview.note: Progesterone rises after ovulation and peaks mid-luteal.
Appetite and energy intake tend to be higher in the luteal phase, and “may” keeps the wording appropriately soft.
sources: Reviews of the menstrual cycle and energy balance (e.g. Davidsen et al., Obes Rev 2007): energy intake and appetite tend to be higher in the luteal phase

copyReview.note: Fibre-rich whole carbohydrates give a smaller blood-sugar rise than refined ones. Evidence that this matters more in the luteal phase is limited, so present it as general nutrition.
sources: EU Register of nutrition and health claims, Regulation (EU) No 432/2012: authorised health-claim wording
